title: "Brunei's prices stopped rising by 2025, but stayed 7% above 2019"
description: "Have prices recovered from the pandemic years, and have they stabilised?"
number: "01"
topic: "Economy"
data-period: "2015–2025"

```{python}
import sys

from shared.glossary import glossary_popovers
from shared.components import (
    chart_card,
    method_and_sources,
    prev_next,
    related_studies,
    stat_tile,
    stat_tiles,
)
from shared.outputs import read_output
from shared.paths import CASE_STUDIES, REPO_URL, ROOT

STUDY = CASE_STUDIES / "01_cost_of_living"
sys.path.insert(0, str(STUDY / "analysis"))
import figures as F  # noqa: E402

change, prov_change, _ = read_output(STUDY / "outputs" / "cpi_change.csv")
index, prov_index, notes_index = read_output(STUDY / "outputs" / "cpi_index.csv")
summary, prov_summary, _ = read_output(STUDY / "outputs" / "cpi_summary_2025.csv")
items, prov_items, notes_items = read_output(STUDY / "outputs" / "subsidised_prices.csv")
check, prov_check, notes_check = read_output(STUDY / "outputs" / "cpi_crosscheck.csv")

chg = change.pivot(index="year", columns="category", values="pct_change")
since = summary.set_index("category")["change_since_2019_pct"]
ALL, FOOD = "Overall CPI", "Food and Non-Alcoholic Beverages"


def avg(cat, a, b):
    return chg.loc[a:b, cat].mean()


def pct(v, d=1):
    return f"{v:+.{d}f}%".replace("-", "−")


all_2025, food_2025 = chg.loc[2025, ALL], chg.loc[2025, FOOD]
all_since, food_since = since[ALL], since[FOOD]
before_avg, pandemic_avg, recent_avg = avg(ALL, 2016, 2019), avg(ALL, 2020, 2022), avg(ALL, 2023, 2025)
recent_lo, recent_hi = chg.loc[2023:2025, ALL].min(), chg.loc[2023:2025, ALL].max()
peak_2022, food_2023 = chg.loc[2022, ALL], chg.loc[2023, FOOD]
cats_2025 = chg.loc[2025].drop(ALL)
n_up, n_down = int((cats_2025 > 0).sum()), int((cats_2025 < 0).sum())
w = items.pivot(index="item", columns="year", values="price_bnd")
VEG = "Vegetable Oil (5 Kg Bottle)"
veg_2019, veg_2022, veg_2025 = w.loc[VEG, 2019], w.loc[VEG, 2022], w.loc[VEG, 2025]
THAI = "Ordinary Thai Rice (10 Kilogramme Bag)"
rice = (w.loc[THAI, 2025] / w.loc[THAI, 2019] - 1) * 100
veg_since = (veg_2025 / veg_2019 - 1) * 100
by_cat = since.drop(ALL)
n_within = int((by_cat.abs() <= 4).sum())
ratio = food_since / all_since
wb = check.dropna(subset=["worldbank_index"])
gap_recent = (wb[wb.year >= 2018].datagovbn_index - wb[wb.year >= 2018].worldbank_index).abs().max()
gap_early = (wb[wb.year < 2018].datagovbn_index - wb[wb.year < 2018].worldbank_index).abs().max()
yr = wb[wb.year >= 2020]
gap_change = (yr.datagovbn_change_pct - yr.worldbank_change_pct).abs().max()
```

::: {.study-intro}
This case study looks at **how prices in Brunei changed from 2015 to 2025**, using the
government's [consumer price index (CPI)]{.term term="cpi"} and average prices of subsidised and price-controlled
items. It compares three periods: before the pandemic (2016–2019), the pandemic years and after
(2020–2022), and the most recent years (2023–2025). It shows **when and what changed, not why**.

It asks two questions, answered in the conclusion:

1. **Have prices recovered from the pandemic years?**
2. **Have they stabilised?**
:::

```{python}
stat_tiles(
    stat_tile("All items, 2024 → 2025", pct(all_2025), "", f"Pre-pandemic average: {pct(before_avg)} a year"),
    stat_tile("All items, 2019 → 2025", pct(all_since), "", "Total change over six years"),
    stat_tile("Food & drink, 2019 → 2025", pct(food_since), "", "Total change over six years"),
)
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="What “All items” means"}
**All items** is the overall consumer price index. It is not a simple average of the
categories: each category counts according to how much households typically spend on it. So a
large rise in a category households spend little on moves "All items" less than a smaller rise
in one they spend a lot on. The source doesn't publish these spending shares.
:::

```{python}
fig, table = F.annual_change(change)
chart_card(
    fig,
    title=f"Price rises peaked at {pct(peak_2022)} in 2022 and have been flat since 2023",
    subtitle="Yearly change in consumer prices, all items (%) · 2016–2025",
    alt=(
        f"Bar chart of yearly price change. Small changes either side of zero from 2016 to 2019, "
        f"rises of about 2% in 2020 and 2021 and {pct(peak_2022)} in 2022, then changes between "
        f"{pct(recent_lo)} and {pct(recent_hi)} from 2023 to 2025."
    ),
    provenance=prov_change,
    table=table,
)
```

## Price growth and price levels, 2015–2025

"Recovered" can mean two things, so both are measured here. **Price growth** is how fast prices
are rising each year: from 2023 to 2025 it averaged `{python} pct(recent_avg)` a year, against
`{python} pct(before_avg)` in 2016–2019 and `{python} pct(pandemic_avg)` in 2020–2022.

**Price level** is how high prices are compared with 2019. From 2019 to 2025, all items rose
`{python} pct(all_since)` and food and drink `{python} pct(food_since)`. The yearly decrease in
2025 (`{python} pct(all_2025)`) is small next to those rises.

```{python}
fig, table = F.level_vs_base(index)
chart_card(
    fig,
    title="Both lines levelled off above their 2019 level, food much higher",
    subtitle="Consumer prices relative to 2019 (2019 = 100) · 2015–2025",
    alt=(
        f"Line chart. All items and food and drink both sit near 100 until 2019, rise through "
        f"2022, then flatten. In 2025 all items are {pct(all_since)} and food and drink "
        f"{pct(food_since)} above 2019."
    ),
    provenance=prov_index,
    table=table,
)
```

## Change by category, 2019 → 2025

`{python} n_within` of the `{python} len(by_cat)` categories are within 4% of their 2019 level.
Food and drink and miscellaneous goods and services stand out, while communication and clothing are slightly
cheaper than in 2019.

```{python}
fig, table = F.since_base_by_category(summary)
chart_card(
    fig,
    title=f"Food & drink rose {ratio:.1f}× as much as prices overall",
    subtitle="Change in prices by category, 2019 → 2025 (%)",
    alt=(
        f"Horizontal bar chart of change since 2019 by category. Miscellaneous and food and "
        f"drink rose most; communication and clothing fell. All items: {pct(all_since)}."
    ),
    provenance=prov_summary,
    table=table,
    height=420,
)
```

### How each category moved over time

Each panel shows one category (turquoise) against all items (grey), [relative to 2019]{.term term="index-rebased"}. The
shaded band marks 2020–2022. Food rose steadily through the shaded years and kept rising in
2023 (`{python} pct(food_2023)`) before levelling off, while transport rose sharply in 2021–2022
and has fallen every year since.

```{python}
fig, table = F.category_timelines(index)
chart_card(
    fig,
    title="Most categories levelled off after 2022; food was one of the last",
    subtitle=(
        "Consumer prices by category relative to 2019 (2019 = 100) · 2015–2025 · "
        "each title shows the change 2019 → 2025"
    ),
    alt=(
        "Eleven small line charts, one per category, each compared with all items. Food and "
        "drink and miscellaneous rise furthest above 2019; communication and clothing end "
        "below it."
    ),
    provenance=prov_index,
    table=table,
    height=640,
    mobile_fig=F.category_timelines(index, cols=2)[0],
    mobile_height=920,
)
```

## Subsidised and price-controlled items, 2019 → 2025

The government publishes average prices for subsidised and price-controlled staples.
Vegetable oil rose from BND `{python} f"{veg_2019:.2f}"` for a 5 kg bottle in 2019 to
`{python} f"{veg_2022:.2f}"` in 2022, and was still `{python} f"{veg_2025:.2f}"` in 2025. Rice
prices, by contrast, moved very little: ordinary Thai rice was `{python} pct(rice)` over the
same six years.

```{python}
fig, table = F.subsidised_since_base(items)
chart_card(
    fig,
    title=f"Vegetable oil cost {veg_since:.0f}% more in 2025 than in 2019",
    subtitle="Change in average retail price, 2019 → 2025 (%)",
    alt=(
        "Horizontal bar chart of price change since 2019 for subsidised items. Vegetable oil "
        "rose most, then palm oil, infant formula and corn oil; rice changed little and sugar fell."
    ),
    provenance=prov_items,
    table=table,
    height=420,
)
```

## How much prices moved in 2023–2025

To judge stability, this section looks at the size of recent yearly changes. Overall price
changes in 2023–2025 stayed between `{python} pct(recent_lo)` and `{python} pct(recent_hi)`,
compared with `{python} pct(chg.loc[2016:2019, ALL].min())` to
`{python} pct(chg.loc[2016:2019, ALL].max())` in 2016–2019. In 2025, `{python} n_up` categories
rose and `{python} n_down` fell, and none moved by more than about 1%. Food and drink rose
`{python} pct(food_2023)` in 2023, then `{python} pct(chg.loc[2024, FOOD])` in 2024 and
`{python} pct(food_2025)` in 2025, its first yearly decrease since 2019.

## Conclusion

- **Have prices recovered from the pandemic years?** Price *growth* has: from 2023 to 2025 prices changed by an average
  of `{python} pct(recent_avg)` a year, back near the pre-pandemic `{python} pct(before_avg)`.
  Price *levels* haven't: from 2019 to 2025, all items rose `{python} pct(all_since)` and food
  and drink `{python} pct(food_since)`, and they have not come back down.
- **Have they stabilised?** Yes. Overall yearly changes in 2023–2025 stayed between
  `{python} pct(recent_lo)` and `{python} pct(recent_hi)`, a narrower range than before the
  pandemic. Food settled last, with its first yearly decrease in 2025.
- **At the shop:** cooking oils are still well above 2019 (vegetable oil
  `{python} pct(veg_since, 0)`, 2019 → 2025), while rice prices barely changed
  (ordinary Thai rice `{python} pct(rice)`).

::: {.callout-caution appearance="simple" title="What this doesn't tell us"}
<!-- Side note: required on every case study (DESIGN.md §4.1). -->
- **Why prices moved.** The 2020–2022 rises line up in time with the pandemic and with
  worldwide price rises in 2022, but this data can't separate causes.
- **What households paid.** These are national annual averages. They don't show differences
  between districts, households or months.
- **Two published values were repaired.** The source CPI table had its 2023 categories shifted
  by one row and a wrong 2022 overall figure. Both were rebuilt from the publisher's own yearly
  % changes and agree closely with World Bank figures (see Method).
- **Base year.** The source doesn't state the CPI base year, so results are shown as changes
  and relative to 2019.
- **Gaps in the item list.** Sugar's 2024 price (BND 1.73, against 1.30 in other years) looks
  implausible and isn't used. "Local Rice" replaced "Laila Rice" in 2020, so neither is
  compared with 2019.
:::
